title: Pilot-to-Production Roadmap
shortDefinition: A documented plan defining the specific milestones an AI proof-of-concept must clear before full deployment.
definition: A pilot-to-production roadmap is a documented plan defining the specific, measurable milestones an AI proof-of-concept or pilot must clear before committing to full production deployment — pre-agreed success criteria, scaling considerations, and decision points that prevent a pilot from either stalling indefinitely in 'pilot purgatory' or rushing to production before genuinely validated. A surprisingly large share of AI pilots never reach production, often not because the underlying technology failed, but because no clear roadmap existed for what 'success' meant or what came next after the pilot phase.

sections.title: Why so many AI pilots stall without reaching production
sections.description: Pilots often stall because success criteria are never clearly defined, or production-scale considerations are overlooked.

content.text: A common pattern: an AI pilot is launched with enthusiasm but without pre-defined, specific success criteria — when the pilot concludes, there's no clear, objective basis for deciding whether to proceed to production, leading to ambiguous results getting debated rather than acted upon, and the project quietly losing momentum. Separately, pilots are sometimes tested only at small scale without considering what genuinely changes at production volume (inference cost, latency under real load, data pipeline reliability), leading to unpleasant surprises if a 'successful' pilot is then naively scaled up without addressing these production-specific considerations.

items: No success criteria — ambiguous results get debated indefinitely.
Project stall — momentum is lost without a clear decision.
Scale oversight — pilot cost ≠ production cost.
Production surprises — cost, latency, reliability issues at scale.
Common pattern — many pilots fail to reach production.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: A surprisingly large share of AI pilots never reach production — often not because the technology failed, but because no clear roadmap existed for what 'success' meant.

sections.title: What a solid pilot-to-production roadmap defines

content.text: A thorough roadmap establishes specific, measurable success criteria before the pilot begins (not retroactively chosen based on whatever results look favorable), a realistic assessment of what changes at production scale (cost, infrastructure, monitoring requirements), a clear decision framework for go/no-go after the pilot concludes, and a defined incremental rollout plan (rather than an all-at-once production launch) that allows catching unexpected issues at limited scale before full exposure. This structure transforms an ambiguous 'see how it goes' pilot into a genuinely decision-useful exercise.

items: Success criteria — specific, measurable, defined upfront.
Scale assessment — realistic production cost and infrastructure.
Decision framework — clear go/no-go criteria.
Incremental rollout — catch issues before full exposure.
Actionable outcome — transforms ambiguity into clear decisions.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of pilot-to-production planning

content.text: Pilot-to-production planning has limitations. Success criteria defined upfront may not fully anticipate all real-world complexities. Production costs can still differ from projections due to unforeseen usage patterns. Pilot data may not fully represent production data diversity, and infrastructure requirements can be underestimated. Incremental rollout can extend timeline, and even with a solid plan, organizational inertia or competing priorities can still delay production deployment. Roadmaps need periodic review as business conditions change.

items: Upfront criteria — may not anticipate all real-world complexities.
Cost uncertainty — production costs can still diverge.
Data diversity — pilot data may not reflect production variety.
Infrastructure gaps — requirements can be underestimated.
Timeline extension — incremental rollout adds time.
Organizational factors — inertia can still delay deployment.

content.title: Important
content.text: A pilot-to-production roadmap is essential but not a guarantee. Regular review and adaptation are necessary as conditions evolve.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about pilot-to-production roadmaps

items.question: Why do so many AI pilots fail to reach production?
items.answer: Often not because the underlying technology failed, but because no clear, pre-defined success criteria existed to make an objective go/no-go decision, or because production-scale considerations (cost, infrastructure) weren't planned for during the pilot phase.

items.question: What should be defined before an AI pilot even begins?
items.answer: Specific, measurable success criteria, an honest assessment of what changes at production scale, and a clear decision framework for what happens after the pilot concludes — all established before the pilot starts, not retroactively.

items.question: Can ClickMasters help with a pilot that's already stalled without a clear path forward?
items.answer: Yes, ClickMasters can establish retroactive success criteria and a decision framework to provide a clear path to resolution, whether that means proceeding to production or making an informed decision to stop.

items.question: How does a pilot-to-production roadmap account for the cost difference between pilot and production scale?
items.answer: ClickMasters includes realistic production-scale cost projections (inference cost, infrastructure, monitoring) as part of the roadmap, avoiding the common surprise of pilot-stage costs not reflecting actual production economics.

items.question: How long does developing a pilot-to-production roadmap take?
items.answer: 4–10 weeks depending on whether it's upfront planning for a new pilot or recovery planning for an existing stalled project.

items.question: Should production rollout happen all at once, or incrementally?
items.answer: ClickMasters generally recommends incremental rollout, allowing issues to be caught and addressed at limited scale before full production exposure, rather than an all-at-once launch.

items.question: What is 'pilot purgatory' in AI projects?
items.answer: Pilot purgatory is the state where an AI pilot has been completed but no decision has been made about production deployment. The project stalls indefinitely, neither being approved for production nor officially canceled, often due to ambiguous success criteria.

items.question: How do you define success criteria for an AI pilot?
items.answer: Success criteria should be specific, measurable, and tied to business outcomes. Examples: "Reduce manual review time by 30%," "Achieve 95% accuracy on validation data," or "Reduce false positives by 25%." ClickMasters helps define these upfront.

items.question: What is the difference between a pilot and a proof-of-concept?
items.answer: The terms are often used interchangeably. Some distinguish a proof-of-concept as a technical feasibility test (can the model work?), while a pilot is a more realistic test with real users and data (does the model work in practice?). Both need clear success criteria and a production roadmap.

items.question: Can a pilot-to-production roadmap be used for non-AI projects?
items.answer: The principles apply broadly to any technology project, but the specific AI considerations — model validation, inference cost, drift monitoring, and data requirements — make it particularly relevant for AI projects. ClickMasters specializes in AI-specific roadmaps.
